dtss.title: The system boundary
dtss.body: Follow the complete chain: local collection, link sewers, deep conveyance, water reclamation, and the subsequent reuse or discharge pathway. A tunnel does not itself produce NEWater. Its interfaces with treatment capacity and upstream flows are part of the engineering problem.

dtss.title: What must happen before what?
dtss.body: Divide the programme into packages while preserving the connections between them. Access shafts enable tunnel drives; excavation and ring erection precede the additional lining and protection work described in the historical contract. Connecting and commissioning a system is a separate step from finishing a tunnel drive.

dtss.title: The decision worth inspecting
dtss.body: Depth can support gravity conveyance, but deep access increases the importance of maintenance planning. PUB’s isolation gates, corrosion-resistant concrete and fibre-optic monitoring address different lifecycle problems. They are not interchangeable gadgets: isolation, durability and observation each support a different operational need.

dtss.title: How to interrogate a construction plan
dtss.body: Ask where temporary access is required, how adjacent packages meet, how an incomplete downstream system is kept separate from service, and what evidence authorises a handover. These are engineering review questions; public sources here do not provide a complete approved inspection-and-test plan.

dtss.title: What this exhibit cannot establish
dtss.body: It cannot establish an actual invert level, tunnel gradient, cover, hydraulic capacity, corrosion life, exact alignment or construction duration. Those require project-specific design information. The Phase 2 innovation story and the 2001 contract account describe different phases and must not be treated as one identical specification.

mrt.title: A station is an interface machine
mrt.body: The engineering boundary extends from entrances and concourse to platforms, tracks, tunnels, ventilation, power and safe access. The cutaway makes some spatial relationships visible; it does not establish the real depth or arrangement of a named station.

mrt.title: Ground conditions choose the method
mrt.body: LTA describes different tunnel-boring approaches for different ground and groundwater conditions. A useful engineering question is how face support, spoil removal, segment erection and surface settlement are considered together. There is no single machine setting or excavation method that can safely be generalised across the whole island.

mrt.title: Building beside a working city
mrt.body: Existing buildings, utilities and operating transport limit what can be moved or interrupted. LTA’s accounts of ground freezing and monitoring show why some interfaces need local treatment. Ground freezing is a documented solution at particular TEL works, not an assertion that every MRT station uses it.

mrt.title: Sequence and verification
mrt.body: The model separates excavation support, structural floors, railway fit-out and public-use equipment. This is an explanatory dependency order, not a station contractor’s programme. Review questions include movement limits, temporary support removal, installation access, system integration and readiness for passenger service.

mrt.title: An honest network history
mrt.body: The first public MRT service began in 1987. A 2000 snapshot can therefore state that the network existed, but a precise map needs dated line and station data. This exhibit deliberately does not turn the present-day schematic into a purported historical alignment.

tuas.title: Start with the operational requirement
tuas.body: Port capacity is useful only when ships, quay cranes, yard storage, internal transport and landside connections work together. MPA’s account connects ground performance with automated guided vehicle operation. Stable terminal ground is therefore part of an automation strategy, not simply an earlier civil works concern.

tuas.title: The caisson dependency chain
tuas.body: The representative chain is fabrication, preparation for marine transport, seabed preparation, placement and integration with reclaimed ground. Floating and positioning a large unit are temporary conditions with different concerns from its final service condition. This exhibit separates these steps conceptually; it does not reproduce a marine lifting or towing plan.

tuas.title: Making fill perform
tuas.body: MPA describes reusing excavated material and stabilising softer material. The planning question is how material availability, treatment, placement, settlement and terminal tolerances fit together. It is misleading to describe reclamation as merely tipping sand into water and then placing an automated terminal on top.

tuas.title: Where packages meet
tuas.body: Inspect the handovers between marine works, reclamation, pavement, crane infrastructure, power and automated systems. Ask which tolerances each receiving package depends on, and which can be monitored after handover. These are an independent planning framework, not a disclosed list of Tuas contract acceptance criteria.

tuas.title: Read the dates as different promises
tuas.body: Opening in 2022, subsequent phased operation, eventual 65 million TEU annual capacity, full development in the 2040s and an operational net-zero ambition by 2050 are distinct statements. None means the entire future port was already complete in 2026. The generic terminal model is not the whole Tuas layout.

newater.title: Separate collection from purification
newater.body: DTSS collects and conveys used water; reclamation treats it; NEWater applies further purification. Presenting these as connected systems explains why resilience depends on multiple facilities and interfaces. The exhibit is a process schematic rather than a piping and instrumentation diagram.

newater.title: Three treatment barriers
newater.body: PUB describes microfiltration or ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and ultraviolet disinfection. The explanatory sequence lets a visitor separate membrane pre-treatment, dissolved-substance removal and final disinfection. It does not calculate removal performance, membrane flux, UV dose or the quality of a sample.

newater.title: The innovation is also a qualification process
newater.body: PUB’s history describes an earlier investigation, a later reconsideration as technology matured, demonstration around 2000 and the first factories in 2003. Moving from a plausible process to public infrastructure includes evidence-building and operational confidence; an idea alone does not establish a dependable supply.

newater.title: A planning lens for the plant
newater.body: Ask about the quality and variability of incoming water, membrane protection, maintenance access, energy, replacement cycles, monitoring and interfaces with users. These are general process-engineering questions. This repository has no plant-specific performance guarantee or commissioned operating envelope.

newater.title: Do not universalise a trial
newater.body: Later accounts discuss technologies such as membrane bioreactors and flow reversal in particular development contexts. A published trial or improvement is not evidence that every NEWater facility already uses the same configuration. The model shows the public high-level treatment sequence only.

barrage.title: One structure, several operating aims
barrage.body: Marina Barrage combines water supply, flood management and recreation. The engineering story is about operating conditions as much as structural form. The nine-gate illustration explains the public description, while the surrounding arrangement remains generic.

barrage.title: The boundary condition is the tide
barrage.body: PUB describes gravity release through crest gates at low tide and pumping when high sea levels prevent that route. A clear explanation should therefore distinguish the upstream catchment, reservoir water level and downstream sea level. Opening a gate is not a universal answer to every storm condition.

barrage.title: Commissioning is not one date
barrage.body: The barrage opened in 2008 and the reservoir became freshwater in 2010. Physical completion, changes in the water body and readiness for a particular use can be separate milestones. A project timeline should preserve these distinctions.

barrage.title: Questions for an integrated plan
barrage.body: Ask how water-control equipment can be inspected or maintained, how gates and pumps are coordinated, and how public access relates to operating infrastructure. This notebook provides a planning lens, not control logic, emergency procedures or a validated flood-routing model.

barrage.title: Scale that the exhibit leaves unresolved
barrage.body: Actual pump duty, design storms, reservoir operations and structural loads require their own source-backed engineering inputs. The visible movement and sectional arrangement should never be interpreted as a forecast of flood protection under a particular event.

reclamation.title: Two different ways to make usable land
reclamation.body: Conventional reclamation raises a platform using fill. A polder encloses an area with a dike and manages water within it. HDB’s account of the Pulau Tekong polder describes the land addition and sand-saving rationale. The model makes the enclosure and drainage relationship visible without depicting internal military facilities.

reclamation.title: An enclosure creates an operating responsibility
reclamation.body: A dike, drains, a collection pond and pumping are a connected system. The design question extends beyond the initial volume of imported sand to how water will be managed throughout the asset life. The public source supports the polder concept, not this exhibit’s generic dimensions.

reclamation.title: The sequence has dependencies
reclamation.body: The enclosure and water-management arrangements must be considered alongside ground preparation and later land use. Showing these as separate steps helps explain why a reclamation programme cannot be reduced to a single area number. The order shown is representative and does not establish the actual package schedule.

reclamation.title: Land-making changes lived geography
reclamation.body: NLB’s accounts of East Coast reclamation and Siglap connect engineering work with changing shorelines and communities. The planning story should include existing access and uses, not only new development capacity. A credible historical coastline needs dated evidence; a present orientation polygon cannot substitute for it.

reclamation.title: Future proposals are separate decisions
reclamation.body: An operating polder does not prove that every future reclamation proposal will use the same method. Site conditions, intended use, material supply and water-management requirements matter. The 2050 view is an explicitly labelled planning scenario.

coast.title: Define the problem before drawing an island
coast.body: PUB’s coastal studies and URA’s Long Island material connect protection, drainage, land use and recreation. The relevant boundary includes the coast and inland catchments. A defence that blocks the sea also has to consider water coming from the land.

coast.title: Alternatives carry different burdens
coast.body: Public material contrasts options involving coastal walls and drainage controls with the Long Island concept. Compare protection, pumping, public access, land use and the shoreline experience together. A drawing that only shows additional land conceals these operating and spatial trade-offs.

coast.title: Preparatory work is not the final project
coast.body: URA’s September 2026 update schedules preparatory reclamation from end-2026 and explicitly distinguishes its area from the final Long Island profile. The 3D islands are therefore envisioned generic geometry. They must not be read as a traced official island outline or an as-built condition.

coast.title: Programme around existing activities
coast.body: The update describes phasing around the area west and east of Bedok Jetty, with the eastern part following the 2029 Southeast Asian Games. Existing activities can affect programme logic before the main permanent works are fully defined. That is a concrete example of planning beyond structural calculations.

coast.title: A 2050 question, not a completion claim
coast.body: The timeline’s future lens asks what protection and drainage systems may be needed; it does not invent a 2050 Long Island deadline. Ground investigation, technical studies, environmental understanding, consultation and later decisions remain relevant evidence gaps for a detailed project reconstruction.

caverns.title: Move a use, release a surface
caverns.body: JTC describes underground hydrocarbon storage as a way to conserve valuable surface land. The story is about three-dimensional land use: a storage requirement can be accommodated below ground while other economic activity uses the surface.

caverns.title: Access constrains excavation
caverns.body: An underground chamber depends on access and construction logistics before it can become usable storage space. The model separates access, excavation, support and fit-out. It does not reproduce actual shaft coordinates, cavern topology, ground support or the containment design.

caverns.title: Planning can be as consequential as digging
caverns.body: JTC describes a fifteen-year journey comprising six years of planning and nine of construction. This is useful evidence against treating a major underground asset as only a tunnelling programme. Feasibility, site understanding, interfaces and the end use are part of making the project possible.

caverns.title: Review the whole storage system
caverns.body: A technically useful review asks how geology, excavation stability, access, containment, operations and surface interfaces are assessed together. The exhibit does not disclose operating procedures or assert a particular containment mechanism beyond the sources actually represented.

caverns.title: Read the headline measurements carefully
caverns.body: The sourced 150-metre depth, 1.47-million-cubic-metre storage volume and surface-land saving describe different dimensions of value. The schematic is deliberately compact and exaggerated for visibility; a measurement taken from it is not evidence of a real chamber cross-section.

power.title: The lifecycle reason for a tunnel
power.body: SP’s account links dedicated cable tunnels with long-term reliability and easier cable installation or replacement while reducing repeated disruption at the surface. The civil tunnel and the cables it accommodates have related but different renewal cycles.

power.title: Civil access before network fit-out
power.body: The representative sequence separates shaft access, tunnel excavation and lining, cable supports, then cable installation. This shows the dependency between civil space and the electricity equipment using it. The drawing contains no real electrical network topology.

power.title: Make maintenance a spatial problem
power.body: Cable support, inspection access and replacement logistics need physical room. The cross-section invites a visitor to inspect that relationship. Rack spacing, cable count and clearance in this model are invented illustrative geometry, not disclosed design standards.

power.title: Construction and service are separate milestones
power.body: An earlier SP article describes construction from 2012 and a forward-looking completion programme. The later sustainability report confirms completion in 2019. The timeline uses the later evidence for completion rather than recycling an old forecast as a fact.

power.title: Boundaries of public explanation
power.body: The project can explain why underground utility space is useful without publishing exact routes, access locations, live circuit arrangements or protection settings. The 2050 lens discusses the value of maintainable infrastructure; it does not predict the future network configuration.
